content: The guideline development process involved the establishment of two additional groups: the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group. The WHO Guideline Development Group for Micronutrients was formed for the 2010–2011 biennium to advise WHO on selecting critical outcomes for decision-making within the scope of the guideline. Another group, the WHO Guideline Development Group for Nutrition Actions, was established for the 2013–2014 biennium to review evidence, deliberate on its interpretation, and formulate recommendations. The WHO Guideline Development Groups included experts from various WHO expert advisory panels and specialists identified through open calls, ensuring a balanced gender mix, multidisciplinary expertise, and representation from all WHO regions. Efforts were made to include content experts, methodologists, stakeholders (such as healthcare managers and professionals), and technical staff from WHO and Member States' health ministries. Representatives of commercial organizations were excluded from membership in these groups. External technical experts in food fortification and review authors participated only in open meetings and recused themselves during deliberations. The final draft guideline underwent peer review by six content experts who provided technical feedback. These reviewers were identified through expert panels within and outside WHO. External peer reviewers were not involved in the guideline development process but were asked to comment on the final draft, focusing on identifying errors, missing data, clarity, and implementation implications without altering the recommendations formulated by the guideline development group. Peer reviewers acted in their individual capacity and completed a declaration-of-interests form, while reviewers representing organizations were exempt from this requirement. Their names and affiliations were acknowledged but did not imply endorsement of the recommendations. The guideline's scope, evidence appraisal, and decision-making process began with drafting key questions using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Control, Outcomes) format. These questions were reviewed and modified by the WHO Steering Committee and the Guideline Development Group for Micronutrients (2010–2011). The group scored the importance of each outcome on a scale of 1 to 9, with higher scores indicating critical importance for decision-making. The final key questions and critical outcomes were listed in PICO format. In April 2013, WHO, in collaboration with the Sackler Institute for Nutrition Science and the Food Fortification Initiative, convened a non-normative dialogue in New York, USA, to discuss technical considerations for fortifying maize flour and cornmeal. This meeting brought together approximately 60 experts, researchers, producers, policymakers, program implementers, private sector representatives, and civil society members to discuss the technology, feasibility, economic impact, and legislation related to fortification. The results of this meeting were published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. To inform the guideline, WHO commissioned systematic reviews of evidence using Cochrane methodology. Unpublished or ongoing studies were identified by contacting over 10 international organizations working on micronutrient interventions and systematically searching the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No language restrictions were applied. Evidence summaries were prepared using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to assess the overall quality of evidence. These summaries were used to draft the guideline. During the guideline development process, members of the Guideline Development Group completed forms to indicate their positions on recommendations, judgments on harms and benefits, and the strength of recommendations. Deliberations among group members were private, and the WHO Secretariat facilitated the process without voting or veto power. If unanimous consensus was not reached, additional time was allocated for deliberations, followed by online voting. A two-thirds majority was required for approval if consensus was not achieved. Divergent opinions could be recorded in the guideline. Management of competing interests followed WHO rules. All experts declared relevant interests before participation, and declarations were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments. Participants acted in their individual capacity and verbally declared potential conflicts of interest at the start of each meeting. Public notices were issued before meetings, including biographies of participants and the scope and purpose of the guideline development group meeting. Specific declarations of interest were managed transparently. For example, Dr. Hector Bourges Rodriguez, chair of the Dannon Institute in Mexico, declared receiving funds from the institute, which is funded by Dannon Mexico. Since Dannon does not manufacture products related to maize flour and cornmeal fortification, he participated fully in deliberations. Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil, affiliated with the Micronutrient Initiative, recused herself from voting due to her involvement in systematic reviews discussed in the meeting. Dr. Lynette Neufeld, employed by the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, also recused herself from voting. Ms. Carol Tom, employed by USAID and a consultant for ECSA-HC, participated fully as her employment did not present a conflict of interest. The WHO Secretariat will monitor research developments in maize flour and cornmeal fortification, particularly in areas with limited or low-quality evidence. If updates are warranted, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the process following WHO's formal procedures. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, a search for new evidence will be conducted to ensure its validity.
